subject: blueprintSpitfire
pitch:
Category: Vehicle.
Subject: Spitfire fighter plane.
Style: cyanotype blueprint.
reasoning:
I'm planning out a Spitfire fighter plane rendered in cyanotype blueprint style, aiming for a rich part count around 180-340 pieces with 5-12 textures, using deep Prussian blue with pale cyan/white linework throughout since it's a vehicle rather than a creature.

Panel lines, rivets, and roundels get drawn as white linework over blueprint-blue surfaces with a fixed palette of deep blue, mid blue, light cyan, and white. I'm working out the Spitfire Mk I's real dimensions (wingspan ~11.23m, length ~9.12m, height ~3.86m) and figuring out how to pose it on the ground with landing gear down, tail wheel back, and a slight nose-up attitude, building the fuselage as a loft of stations along a centerline that rises gently toward the nose.

Now I'm laying out specific fuselage stations from nose to tail with their z-position, vertical center, width, and height to shape the cowl, cockpit, and tapering tail section, along with wheel sizing for ground contact.

I'm now working out the undercarriage geometry — main wheel radius, fuselage bottom height relative to ground attitude, wing root position, and gear leg length and track width, accounting for the Spitfire's characteristic outward-splaying retractable gear.

Prop diameter around 3.2m with tip near ground when nose-down. For the wing I'm working out an elliptical planform: half-span 5.6m, root chord ~2.55m tapering to a 0.5m tip.

Positioning the wing with the straight-ish leading edge and strongly curved trailing edge typical of the Spitfire, extruding the outline so thickness runs along the vertical axis. A flat plate would be simpler, but I want to taper the airfoil thickness for a more realistic shape.

Thinking through alternatives for building the wing: maybe lofting along the span with stations defining chord width and thickness height at each point, though the cross-section shape and orientation of the loft's width/height axes relative to the flight path are unclear and risky to assume. I'm leaning toward constructing the wing more directly instead.

Decals work on any mesh queried through b.surface, so roundels on wings and fuselage sides fit naturally into the builder. I'm sketching a wing geometry generator: span stations mirrored per side, airfoil-like top/bottom curves with triangulated indices, then flat-shaded normals via toNonIndexed and computeVertexNormals.

Still writing geometry math...

I'm adjusting the elliptical semi-span parameter to get a realistic tapered tip chord, settling on roughly 5.75 as the ellipse's effective span so the tip chord comes out small but not zero, then adding one more rounded tip station near x=5.72 to cap the wing smoothly.

Now I'm working out the quarter-chord line to capture the Spitfire's slight sweep, defining leading and trailing edges relative to it so the root LE sits around z=0.99 and TE around z=-1.56, which helps me place the cockpit and pilot roughly above the wing root near z=-0.3.

For the vertical placement, I'm setting the fuselage and wing so the belly dips slightly below the wing's underside, then applying about 6° of dihedral so the wingtip rises relative to the root — checking that this still lands near realistic tip heights for a Spitfire sitting on its gear.

I'm also working out gear leg lengths, lowering the fuselage stations slightly for a better fit, and recomputing the nose and propeller position relative to ground clearance.

Now I'm thinking about the tail wheel — with the fuselage sitting level, the tail wheel ends up too far below the tail, which doesn't match a realistic tail-down stance. I'm considering tilting the fuselage nose-up to fix this.

Rather than rotating individual parts, it's simpler to build everything level in the aircraft's own frame, then pitch the whole assembly by creating a root joint and applying a rotation to it about the x-axis, letting that single transform carry the fuselage, wings, and tail into the tail-down ground attitude together.

So the plan is: build the airframe level, pose the root joint nose-up 8°, then build the gear afterward in model-space since anything constructed after a pose follows the new orientation. That should let the wheels sit correctly without inheriting the tilt the way earlier-built parts would.

As an alternative to relying on the pose entirely, I'm considering manually computing the tilt myself — defining a helper transform that rotates everything about an axis through the pivot, then applying it explicitly to all my coordinates and custom geometries, including the station points used in lofts and sweeps.

Weighing the effort against the risk, I'll go with b.pose on the root joint since it's well-documented and should handle the rigid parts under one joint cleanly. Now I'm working out the rotation direction: the nose needs to tip up, so I need to figure out whether that requires a positive or negative angle about the x-axis using the right-hand rule.

I also need to decide where the pivot point sits for this rotation — likely at the main wheel axle position, since that's the natural rotation center when the tail lifts, and then I can compute how the rest of the airframe's geometry shifts relative to that pivot once tilted.

Working out the tail wheel leg length from the computed drop, then checking the propeller clearance at the nose and the fin height at the tail using the same rotation math to make sure nothing clips the ground.

I need a mapped helper function so gear positions stay consistent with the tilt transform, rotating about the same pivot point. I'm double-checking the rotation sign convention—negative degrees should raise the nose, which matches tipping the bone about the x-axis at the pivot.

For the moving parts, I'll add a prop joint at the nose pointing forward, then handle the control surfaces. To keep scope manageable, I'll treat rudder, elevators, and ailerons as hinge joints with separate extruded plates sitting on the trailing edges rather than splitting the main wing geometry.

For the look, I'm settling on a full cyanotype blueprint style: deep Prussian blue base with white panel lines, rivet dots, and hatch shading for depth. I'll add blueprint-style decals too, like a roundel rendered as white concentric rings and fuselage code letters as SVG text, similar to Spitfire squadron codes.

I'm also adding technical annotation decals—plane name, scale label, and dimension lines with arrows along the wingspan—plus a faint reference grid with stronger lines every few meters for authenticity. For the panel lines themselves, I'm defining a paint function that mottles the blue surface slightly and draws pale grid lines, with custom panel-line placement along fuselage stations.

Working out seam placement using the aircraft-frame position before pose is applied, so ring seams follow z-position and longitudinal seams follow angle bands near specific degree marks, plus rivet dots along those seams. Now extending this to the wing geometry, placing spanwise rib lines based on position along the wing.

Instead of gun ports as painted circles, I'll model them as tiny protruding stub tubes near the leading edge, sized and positioned using the wing's LE geometry, then move on to fuselage details.

Now I'm working out the cockpit canopy: a loft/sweep from the windscreen front to the rear fairing, with cross-section stations defining width and height rising above the fuselage top, rendered as light cyan glass with white frame lines.

Still drafting the canopy frame geometry...

I'll add side rails at angles near ±70 using the built surface paths, swept thin. For the loft call, I need to check its API — stations are objects with position, width, and height, and options likely include color, bone, sides, and section shape; I'll use something like 12 sides to approximate the oval fuselage cross-section typical of a Spitfire.

Actually, since I'm unsure whether loft forwards options like sides reliably, it's safer to build the fuselage with a sweep instead — passing a catmull-rom path through the centerline stations and a radius function that interpolates rx/ry values along the length, computed from arc-length position.

I need to figure out the direction convention: running the path from tail to nose (so direction is +z) keeps the frame's normal pointing up, avoiding orientation flips. The radius function will sample the path's z position and interpolate the station width/height data at that z, with rounded caps at the nose and a pointed cap at the tail.

I'm thinking the nose needs a cowl lip or spinner ring added in front since the propeller spinner covers the fuselage front, so I'll use a flat cap there and build a separate lathe-generated cowling piece. The fuselage's elliptical cross-sections are simplified compared to the real Spitfire's deep belly, but I'll leave the radiators under the wings for now and consider whether a cockpit cutout or pilot head detail is worth adding.

I'll skip adding a visible pilot since the canopy will be opaque rather than translucent glass, making interior detail pointless. For the cowling, I want to add the row of exhaust stacks characteristic of the Merlin engine -- six small pipes per side positioned along the cowl sides near mid-fuselage, placing them by raycasting inward from outside the fuselage surface to find the correct mounting points at each z-position.

I'll use small cylinders oriented along the surface normal to stick as exhaust stubs, colored a lighter cyan to fit the blueprint palette, and I'll add a couple of thin elongated bump shapes on the cowl top to represent the cylinder head blisters found on the real Merlin cowling.

Now I'm positioning the radiators: the oil cooler goes under the left/port wing (model's +X side) and the larger glycol radiator under the starboard wing, both built as tapered boxes near the wing leading edge and sized relative to the wing's underside height.

Sizing the radiator and oil cooler scoops under the wing with tapered frustum boxes, with the starboard radiator slightly larger than the oil cooler on the port side, and considering a grille texture or outline for the front face.

Now I'm adding wingtip lights and a pitot tube rod extending forward from the port wing leading edge, then moving to the tailplane: an elliptical shape with a 3.2 span, tapering chord from 1.1 at root to 0.5 at tip, reusing the wing geometry builder with a thinner airfoil profile, and setting up the vertical fin similarly.

I'm working out how to reuse this builder for the fin by rotating the geometry 90° around the Z-axis so the span runs vertically, keeping only one symmetric half from the root upward, then thinking through how control surfaces like the rudder should be constructed as separate hinged pieces rather than cutting the main surface.

Now I'm figuring out a parameterized airfoil builder that takes a chord-fraction range so I can generate partial sections for elevators and ailerons—cosine-spacing points between the start and end fractions, closing the geometry with a flat front or back edge and end caps, then placing hinge pivots along that cut line for the rudder, elevators, and ailerons.

For the main wing, I'm handling the notch where ailerons attach by letting the chord cutoff vary by spanwise station: full chord elsewhere, but cut back to 0.75 within the aileron's span range, inserting duplicate stations very close together so the transition creates a thin sliver face rather than a smooth skew — simpler to build even if slightly imperfect geometrically.

I'm placing ailerons spanning roughly x=3.2 to 5.1, using paired stations just fractions of a unit apart to mark the sharp transition from full chord to the cutback aileron fraction, then creating the aileron as its own geometry that continues the same shape so it reads as seamless except at the hidden front face. For the hinge, I'm setting up a joint running along the hinge line from inner to outer pivot points, treating it as a rotational joint parented to the body — straightforward since all joints get created before any pose is applied. I'll skip flaps for now and just note a small root fillet could be added to the wing structure later.

Moving on to landing gear, I'm sketching out the main legs as tapered strut rods with oleo scissor links, wheels made from a lathed tire profile plus a hub cap, and gear doors as leaning extruded plates. For the wheel I'm defining a lathe outline (radius vs. axial position) that traces a closed ring cross-section to form the tire shape, sized to match the Spitfire's roughly 26-inch wheels, with the hub cap as a smaller lighter cylinder and a decal plane for spokes on the sides.

For the gear leg geometry, I'm trying to figure out realistic attach and splay positions based on the Spitfire's actual track width (~5.7 ft), estimating a top attach point around x=0.75 and wheel position around x=1.0 so the legs splay slightly outward as they go down toward the wheels.

I'm working out the wheel axle pivot point in model-frame coordinates, treating it as fixed at the same location before and after the pose transform, then connecting it with a slightly raked rod back up to the wing attach point computed in the aircraft's own coordinate frame.

Now I'm computing the tail wheel attachment point by applying the same rotation formula to its aircraft-frame offset, tracking how the nose-up tilt shifts its vertical position.

Working it out, the tail wheel contact point sits roughly 0.55 above ground, so the strut needs to be about 0.45 long with a wheel radius of 0.1 to reach the floor. I'll just use my air() function and a ray cast to confirm the actual ground contact position instead of hand-calculating further.

Now I'm turning to the propeller design -- going with a three-blade setup (like a later Spitfire variant rather than the original two-blade Watts prop), building each blade as an extruded paddle shape radiating from the hub with a pitch twist applied through rotation.

Defining chord direction with pitch angle, then shaping the blade outline as a tapered paddle profile along the radius.

Still shaping the spinner cone...

Now I'm setting up the propeller joint at the nose with the blades and spinner parented to it, then working on the cowling ring and adjusting the fuselage nose profile to get a proper elliptical lip shape rather than a plain circular cross-section.

I'm also planning the spinner backplate disc, trim rings around the cowl at a few stations, and panel band details, then moving on to fuselage features like the fin fillet, tail cone, position lights, and an antenna mast behind the canopy.

I'm placing the aerial mast on the fuselage spine near the cockpit with a thin wire sweep running to the fin tip, then tallying up parts: wings, ailerons, tip plates, rivet rows, exhaust stacks, gun stubs, and ribs to build toward roughly 200 total parts.

Let me keep stacking detail groups: fuselage seam rings, canopy frames, exhaust stacks, cowl blisters, gun stubs, wing panel gun port covers, fuel cap, landing light lens, wing root fillets, radiators, and per-side gear assemblies with legs, fairings, scissor links, wheels, and doors, plus tail surfaces with trim tabs and a three-blade prop with spinner, backplate, and hub rings.

Now I'm also considering decal/texture elements -- roundels on wing top/bottom, fuselage, and fin flash, squadron codes, dimension arrows, a titleblock plate, grille, wheel hub texture, maybe gauge or glass decals, plus stylized touches like a faint blueprint grid base and dashed construction/centerline sweeps extending beyond the airframe.

I'm planning the dimension and centerline details: a thin dashed white-cyan emissive rod running the length of the fuselage beyond the nose and tail, plus wingspan dimension lines with cone arrowheads, tick marks, and a floating text label like "11.23 m" to mimic blueprint annotation style, deciding where to position these so they read clearly without clipping into the model.

Setting ground reference at y=0 so wheel bottoms (main and tail) sit exactly there, with tire radius 0.34 placing the axle center accordingly, and making sure the propeller tip clears the ground at its lowest rotation point.

Tilting the aircraft 9 degrees nose-up, I compute the rotated y and z coordinates for the spinner tip, finding it clears the ground by about 0.735 units. I'm also laying out the longitudinal stations along the fuselage — cowl front, backplate, spinner, and prop plane positions — to pin down where the nose and propeller actually sit in z.

Now I'm sketching out the fuselage cross-section at each station from nose to tail, tracking the center height, width, and depth to shape the taper down to a pointed tail cap. I'm using this to figure out where the fuselage bottom sits at the wing root station.

I'm checking the wing root geometry against the fuselage profile—computing where the wing's centerline and thickness fall relative to the fuselage cross-section, and finding the leading and trailing edge positions along the fuselage. It looks like the wing bottom lines up closely with the fuselage bottom at that station, consistent with how a Spitfire's narrow fuselage sits above the low-mounted wing.

I'm working out the elliptical planform's chord distribution and thickness taper from root to tip, then deriving the leading and trailing edge curves from a constant quarter-chord line. With the elliptical chord shrinking outboard, the leading edge sweeps back while the trailing edge sweeps forward—matching the Spitfire's distinctive sharply forward-raked trailing edge.

I'm also laying out the dihedral curve for the wing tip and sketching out a station array along the span, placing extra stations near the aileron break for a smoother wing surface.

For the airfoil cross-sections I need consistent point counts across stations even as the chord cut shrinks, so I'm mapping chord fractions using a cosine spacing scaled by the local cut value, then evaluating the airfoil shape at that absolute fraction within each station's chord.

For closing off the cut edge I'm forming a loop with upper points k=0..M and lower points reversed, being careful to avoid duplicating the leading-edge point since both upper and lower surfaces meet there with zero thickness.

I'm skinning consecutive ring sections with quads, triangulated, skipping the root cap since it's hidden inside the fuselage at the mirror plane, and fanning a cap from the centroid at the tip. For the negative-x side I'll mirror the geometry by scaling, which means I need to flip the index order to fix the winding direction.

Normals should come from flattening the geometry to non-indexed and computing vertex normals for a faceted look. I'm also considering adding a basic planar UV mapping based on x and z coordinates, in case painted parts need UVs to avoid defaulting to [0,0].

Now I'm sketching the cyanotype color palette, moving from deep Prussian blue through mid-tones up to pale sky blue for the design.

Writing paint functions...

Writing fuselage paint function...

I'm also layering in a faint blueprint-style grid on dominant surface planes for that cyanotype paper look, plus diagonal hatching on lower, shadowed surfaces to suggest technical shading.

Now I'm capping the flat color palette and moving on to designing the roundel texture as an SVG with concentric circles, light fills, and crosshair center lines in that classic blueprint style.

For the wing roundel I'll reuse the same texture without yellow for the underside version, and the fin flash as a rectangle with three vertical colored bands and outline strokes. For the fuselage code I'm adding serif bold text like "KL·B" in white with a stroke outline, transparent cut outside the circle shapes.

I'm also planning small decal title blocks—one near the tail with scale and drawing number text, and dimension arrows on the wing tops showing wingspan and chord measurements with arrowhead lines and centered labels, oriented along the wing's tilted surface.

Figuring out the correct "up" vector for these decals so the text renders upright and readable from a viewer's perspective looking down at the wing, considering handedness for left/right orientation.

Now I'm planning the remaining decal textures: horizontal bar grilles for the radiators, a spoked wheel hub disc, and a small "ROLLS-ROYCE MERLIN" cowl label. I'm also considering whether the canopy glass needs a sheen texture or if simple paint highlights suffice.

Counting up the stencils so far — roundel, fin flash, fuselage code, title, dimension lines, grille, hub — that's seven, and I'm adding an eighth "NO STEP" walkway stencil near the wing root to round things out, while skipping gun ports and gauge details as unnecessary. I'm also thinking about whether to add a subtle glow to the luminous white dimension lines and roundel edges for the blueprint look.

Since glow should only apply to flat or textured parts (not raw paint), and I'm unsure every decal part guarantees a standard material, I'm wrapping the glow call in a safe helper that falls back to the unmodified part if it throws, so a material mismatch won't break the whole build.

Setting up the imports and core builder utilities...

Defining a sheen paint helper that blends colors based on surface normal and noise for uneven exposure, then starting on a glint overlay function...

Writing grid overlay logic...

Writing fuselage paint logic...

I need to normalize the clock angle so it wraps correctly around 0/360, then handle the symmetric line placements on either side of the tube without conflict at the top seam.

Adding a horizontal split line at 90 and 270 for the waist seam. For rivets, I'm placing dots periodically along both the ring seams and longitudinal seams using fractional offsets based on angle and z-position, keeping spacing small enough to avoid visible aliasing given the texel density.

With a total painted area around 80 m² across fuselage, wings, and tail, I calculate the texel density needs a 2048 paint size to keep seam lines and rivet dots at reasonable pixel widths — so I'll limit painted detail to just the fuselage, wings, tail, and canopy, leaving gear, wheels, and prop as flat colors to keep density manageable.

Now I'm working out the wing paint function based on chord position and spanwise fraction, placing ribs at 0.55m intervals and chordwise panel lines at specific fractions (LE panel, spar line, aileron hinge region), plus rectangular gun bay doors near the leading edge.

Adding the fuel tank access panel outline, a rivet pattern along ribs and chord lines, and a top/underside distinction based on surface normal sign. Starting to define the airfoil geometry generator with station data and a half-thickness function...

Still writing the foil function...

Still working out the ring geometry...

Other surfaces follow the same pattern: aileron and elevator use a fixed hinge fraction while the main wing's chord fraction varies continuously along the cut region, and rudder has its own constant fraction. Now I'm working out the mesh indexing, building quad faces by connecting adjacent ring vertices across stations.

For the triangle winding, I need to check cross products of the ring-direction and span-direction vectors to make sure normals point outward on the top surface, flipping the order when the computed normal points down instead of up.

Working through the implementation detail where I swap two indices when side is negative to correct winding, then moving to the tip cap triangulation—figuring out the correct outward normal direction for the fan triangles by computing cross products of ring vertices relative to the centroid, viewed from the +x direction looking back toward -x.

I conclude the ring winds clockwise from that viewpoint, so I need to reverse the triangle order for counterclockwise outward-facing normals, flipping again for the opposite side. I also decide to make capping optional at each end (capStart, capEnd flags) rather than always capping, since the wing root cap sits inside the fuselage and may not need to be drawn.

Now I'm working out the fin and rudder geometry: since they're built with a local span axis then rotated 90° about z to stand vertically at the fuselage spine, I'm defining their leading edge sweep and chord taper, aiming for a tall, pointed Spitfire-style fin shape.

Still working out the fin's leading/trailing edge taper and chord reduction toward the tip for a rounded shape...

Now I'm figuring out the rudder hinge placement, splitting the fin into a fixed main section (up to ~58% chord) and a rudder section behind it, with the hinge axis running straight from base to tip even as chord varies along the span.

For the tailplane, I'm defining an elliptical chord distribution with root chord around 1.15, working out the leading/trailing edge positions along the quarter-chord line, and setting the elevator hinge at roughly 62% chord, while also fixing the vertical and lateral offset of the tailplane relative to the fuselage centerline.

I'm placing the fin at the fuselage root with its base tucked inside the body, then setting up the wing and rudder geometry parts using absolute aircraft coordinates attached to the body bone. For the joint hierarchy, I'm naming the root joint "body" with a spine-like role and positioning its pivot point accordingly before continuing to define child joints.

Since there's no dedicated "prop" role, I'm using "hinge" for the propeller joint, placed at the nose with its direction aligned along z so blade parts can attach to it, and I'm using the same hinge role for the wheel joints — noting that anything built after the pose transform lands in the new, posed coordinate space.

I'm weighing whether to build the wheel joints after the pose is applied, since that risks complications with how their rotation relative to the tilted parent gets computed, versus an alternative approach where I avoid posing the whole aircraft at all and instead build everything directly in its final orientation, or wrap the root object in a group to apply the tilt separately — trying to figure out which path carries less risk overall.

I'm leaning toward the documented pose-based approach (Option A) since it's well-supported by the harness, even though it means I need to skip creating dedicated wheel joints and instead just attach rigid gear parts directly to the body after posing.

Actually, I realize I could create the joints before the pose step by computing their positions in aircraft-frame coordinates using an inverse mapping, so that after the pose transform they land exactly where I want them in model space. This feels like the cleanest solution since it avoids any post-pose joint creation hacks while keeping everything consistent with the existing joint system.

I verify this matches a -9° rotation about the +X axis, confirming the pose parameters align with my rotation matrix convention. Now I'm double-checking that bones treated as single rigid pieces stay unaffected by this joint change.

I'm not using joint chains here at all—the fuselage is rigid under the body, while child joints like the propeller and control surfaces inherit the body's pose rotation correctly. For the gear, the wheel joints are created before the pose transform at their inverse positions, so I'm tracing through how their local axes (still pointing along X after the tilt) carry forward to the wheel parts built afterward under their own bone frames.

Now I'm sorting which elements get built in aircraft frame versus model frame: wings and radiators attach before the pose, while only the gear—main legs, wheels, doors, and tail wheel/strut—gets built after. I'm transforming the tail wheel attachment point through the pose rotation to get its final aircraft coordinates, computing the strut top and wheel center positions, then confirming the resulting leg length is reasonable. For the fuselage, I'm sweeping a cross-section along a tapered path defined by width/height stations from nose to tail, using smooth interpolation between stations and a catmull-rom spline through the centerline for the sweep path, with a circular cross-section at each point along it.
